title: The seer and the seen
hookLine: He is both the one who sees and what is seen (Sukhmani 23)

cards: Point your phone's camera at a mirror. On the screen you'll see the phone, and in the phone's screen a smaller phone, and inside that a smaller one, shrinking into the distance. The camera is looking at itself looking.

It's a fun trick for about ten seconds, and then it gets a little dizzying. Who's the watcher, and what's being watched? Sukhmani's twenty-third ashtpadi gives a startling answer: God is both, the seer and the seen.

teach.b: Having cleared the eyes and shown God within and without, the twenty-third ashtpadi takes one more step. In paraphrase: God Himself is the one who sees, and God Himself is what is seen.
Gurbani uses this pattern of aap, Himself, often: God Himself the speaker and the listener, the giver and the receiver. In Japji, Guru Nanak says the Creator, having made the world, watches over it.
Sukhmani goes a step further: the watching itself, the light in your eyes, comes from God. Here's one way to feel it.

teach.h: THE TWO ENDS OF EVERY LOOK.
teach.b: Every look has two ends: you, looking, and the thing you look at. Usually we notice only the thing, the tree, the screen, the face, and almost never the looking. Sukhmani says both ends are held by the One.

teach.h: THE LIGHT YOU SEE BY IS HIS.
teach.b: In that picture, the tree is God's play, and the light by which you see it, the jot within, is God's Light too. Drisat is the word for sight or glance.

teach.h: TEACHERS READ IT MORE THAN ONE WAY.
teach.b: Sikh teachers explain this in more than one way, and it's fair to say so. Some stress oneness: there is finally only God, seeing God.
Others stress that God is present in all and yet beyond all, so creature and Creator stay distinct even while the Light is shared. Gurbani holds the mystery without settling it in a slogan.
Either way, in Sukhmani's picture, seeing is not a small, private thing; it's lit by the One.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-third ashtpadi hear that God is both the one who sees and what is seen, and teachers explain this both as oneness and as presence within a God who is also beyond.

o: sight, the glance by which we see
a vision of the future in a dream
a blessing given by touching the head

games.q: the seer and the seen — tap the pairs.

s: Sikh teachers all explain the seer and the seen the same way
some stress oneness; others stress God present in all yet beyond all.
Gurbani often uses aap, Himself, for God at both ends of an act
the speaker and the listener, the giver and the receiver, the seer and the seen.
the practice asks you to stop looking at things
it asks you to notice the looking as well as the thing.

games.q: you're looking at a tree. by the twenty-third ashtpadi, where is God in this moment?
o: at both ends: the seeing and the seen.
games.why: Sukhmani says God is both the one who sees and what is seen. the tree is His play, and the light you see by is His Light.

practice: Look at one thing, a cup, a window, your hand, for a few breaths, and then, without looking away, notice the looking itself: that light is reaching you, that something in you is seeing.
Rest in both at once, coming back to the cup whenever the mind wanders. If you pray, rest in Waheguru as the light you see by.

wordCard.voice: Drisat, sight or glance: Sukhmani says God is at both ends of every drisat: the light that sees, and the world that is seen.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: drisat, sight or glance; Gurbani often pairs it with the seen world.

carryVoice: Your line: lit by the One. Both ends of every look. Day five hundred twenty-eight, done.
